questions.stem: Prove that two chords of a circle are equal in length iff they are equidistant from the center.

hint.level_0: Use the perpendicular from $O$ and Pythagoras.

solution_steps: For a chord, the perpendicular from $O$ bisects it; let the half-chord be $\ell$ and the distance be $d$.
Then $\ell^2+d^2=R^2$ (Pythagoras in the right triangle to an endpoint).
So the chord length $2\ell=2\sqrt{R^2-d^2}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $d$.
Hence equal chords correspond exactly to equal distances $d$.

hint.level_0: Every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$ with $\angle A=50^\circ$, let $I_A$ be the excenter opposite $A$. Prove $\angle BI_AC=65^\circ$.
solution_steps: $I_A$ lies on the internal bisector of $\angle A$ and the external bisectors of $\angle B,\angle C$.
So $\angle I_ABC=90^\circ-\tfrac{\angle B}{2}$ and $\angle I_ACB=90^\circ-\tfrac{\angle C}{2}$ (external bisectors).
Then $\angle BI_AC=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\tfrac{B}{2})-(90^\circ-\tfrac{C}{2})=\tfrac{B+C}{2}=90^\circ-\tfrac{A}{2}.$
Numerically $\angle BI_AC=65^\circ$.

questions.stem: Let $H$ be the orthocenter of acute $\triangle ABC$. Prove the reflection of $H$ in line $BC$ lies on the circumcircle.

hint.level_1: Reflection keeps that angle; use the converse cyclic test.

solution_steps: Reflection in $BC$ preserves angles, so $\angle BH'C=\angle BHC$.
In any triangle $\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle A$.
Thus $\angle BH'C=180^\circ-\angle A$, giving $\angle BH'C+\angle BAC=180^\circ$.
By the converse cyclic condition, $A,B,H',C$ are concyclic, so $H'$ is on the circumcircle.

questions.stem: Prove the circumcenter $O$, centroid $G$, and orthocenter $H$ are collinear with $HG=2\,GO$.
solution_steps: Take $O$ as origin; then $\vec{OH}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}+\vec{OC}$.
The centroid is $\vec{OG}=\tfrac13(\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}+\vec{OC})$.
Hence $\vec{OH}=3\,\vec{OG}$: the three points are collinear.
Then $HG=OH-OG=3\,OG-OG=2\,OG$.

questions.stem: Let $H$ be the orthocenter and $M_a$ the midpoint of $BC$. Prove the reflection of $H$ in $M_a$ is the point of the circumcircle diametrically opposite $A$.

hint.level_0: Use the antipode $A'$ and the semicircle right angles.

solution_steps: Let $A'$ be the antipode of $A$: $\angle ABA'=\angle ACA'=90^\circ$ (angle in semicircle).
Then $A'B\perp AB$ and $CH\perp AB$, so $A'B\parallel CH$; likewise $A'C\parallel BH$.
Hence $BHCA'$ is a parallelogram, so its diagonals $HA'$ and $BC$ bisect each other.
Therefore $M_a$ is the midpoint of $HA'$, i.e. $A'$ is the reflection of $H$ over $M_a$.

hint.level_1: Use the centroid homothety $O\to H$ of ratio $-2$.

From the parallelogram $BHCA'$ (antipode lemma), $HA'=2\,HM_a$ and $O$ is the midpoint of $AA'$.
So $\vec{AH}=\vec{A'A}-\vec{A'H}\Rightarrow$ midline gives $AH=2\,OM_a$.
Equivalently, the homothety at $G$ (ratio $-2$) maps $M_a\to A$ and $O\to H$.

questions.stem: Prove that the three altitude feet, the three side-midpoints, and the three midpoints of $HA,HB,HC$ all lie on one circle (the nine-point circle).

hint.level_0: Two homotheties (at $G$ and at $H$) map known circles onto the same circle.
hint.level_1: Right angles place the feet on it.

solution_steps: Side-midpoints lie on the medial circle (radius $R/2$, center $N$) by the homothety at $G$ of ratio $-\tfrac12$ ($O\to N$).
The homothety at $H$ of ratio $\tfrac12$ maps the circumcircle to the same circle and sends $A,B,C$ to the Euler points $\mathrm{mid}(HA),\dots$.
Each altitude foot lies on the circle with diameter (side-midpoint, Euler point) by its right angle.
All nine points therefore lie on the single circle of radius $R/2$ centered at $N$.

questions.stem: Let $P$ lie on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. Prove the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the three sides are collinear.

hint.level_0: Use the right angles at the feet to find cyclic quadrilaterals.
hint.level_1: Chase directed angles at $X$ and use $P$ on the circumcircle.

solution_steps: Let $X,Y,Z$ be the feet on $BC,CA,AB$. $PXCY$ and $PZBX$ are cyclic (two right angles each).
So $\angle(XP,XY)=\angle(CP,CY)$ and $\angle(XP,XZ)=\angle(BP,BZ)$ (directed angles).
Since $A,B,P,C$ are concyclic, $\angle(CP,CA)=\angle(BP,BA)$.
Combining, $\angle(XY,XP)=\angle(XZ,XP)$, so $X,Y,Z$ are collinear.

solution_steps: By the bisector theorem the foot $D$ divides $BC$ as $BD=\tfrac{ac}{b+c},DC=\tfrac{ab}{b+c}$.
Apply Stewart's theorem with these $m=BD,n=DC$.
Simplify $b^2m+c^2n-a\,mn$ using $m+n=a$.
This collapses to $t_a^2=bc\big(1-\tfrac{a^2}{(b+c)^2}\big)\approx 47.04$.

questions.stem: For a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, prove Ptolemy's relation $AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot BC$.

hint.level_1: Get two similar-triangle relations and add them.

solution_steps: Pick $K$ on $AC$ with $\angle ABK=\angle DBC$.
$\triangle ABK\sim\triangle DBC\Rightarrow AK\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD$.
$\triangle KBC\sim\triangle ABD\Rightarrow KC\cdot BD=AD\cdot BC$.
Add: $AC\cdot BD=(AK+KC)BD=AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot BC$.

questions.stem: Fix $B,C$ and $k\ne1$. Prove that the locus of points $P$ with $PB:PC=k$ is a circle (the Apollonius circle).

hint.level_0: Locate the two points on $BC$ dividing it in ratio $k$.
hint.level_1: These are where the internal/external bisectors of $\angle BPC$ meet $BC$.
hint.level_2: Perpendicular bisectors $\Rightarrow$ right angle $\Rightarrow$ circle on diameter $DE$.

solution_steps: Let $D,E$ on line $BC$ satisfy $DB/DC=EB/EC=k$ (internal/external division).
For any $P$ with $PB/PC=k$, $PD$ and $PE$ bisect $\angle BPC$ internally and externally.
Internal and external bisectors are perpendicular, so $\angle DPE=90^\circ$.
Hence $P$ lies on the circle with diameter $DE$; conversely every such $P$ gives ratio $k$.

questions.stem: The tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ at $B$ and $C$ meet at $T$. Prove that line $AT$ is the $A$-symmedian, meeting $BC$ at the point $S$ with $\dfrac{BS}{SC}=\dfrac{AB^2}{AC^2}$.

hint.level_0: $T$ is the pole of $BC$; use the tangent--chord angle.
hint.level_1: The symmedian is the isogonal of the median; it cuts $BC$ in ratio $c^2:b^2$.

solution_steps: $T$ is the pole of $BC$; $TB=TC$ are equal tangents, and $\angle TBC=\angle BAC$ (tangent--chord).
So $\triangle TBC$ is isosceles and $AT$ is the reflection of the $A$-median over the $A$-bisector (the symmedian).
The symmedian divides $BC$ in the ratio $AB^2:AC^2$ (a standard property of the reflected median).
Hence $A,S,T$ are collinear with $BS/SC=c^2/b^2$.

questions.stem: From an interior point $P$, reflect each cevian $AP,BP,CP$ across the corresponding angle bisector. Prove the three reflected lines are concurrent (the isogonal conjugate $P^\ast$).

hint.level_1: Isogonal reflection inverts each sine ratio.

solution_steps: Reflecting $AP$ over the $A$-bisector keeps the angle to the bisector, so $\angle BAP=\angle CAP^\ast$, etc.
By the trigonometric form of Ceva, $AP,BP,CP$ concurrent $\iff \prod\dfrac{\sin\angle BAP}{\sin\angle CAP}=1$.
The isogonal lines have all these sine ratios inverted, so their product is also $1$.
Hence the reflected cevians are concurrent.

questions.stem: The internal and external bisectors of $\angle A$ meet line $BC$ at $D$ and $E$. Prove that $(B,C;D,E)=-1$, i.e. $D,E$ divide $BC$ harmonically.

hint.level_0: Apply the internal and external angle bisector theorems.
hint.level_1: Internal vs external division flips the sign.

solution_steps: The internal bisector gives $\dfrac{DB}{DC}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$ (angle bisector theorem).
The external bisector gives $\dfrac{EB}{EC}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$ as well, but $E$ divides $BC$ externally.
Thus the two signed ratios are negatives of each other.
Hence the cross ratio $(B,C;D,E)=\dfrac{DB/DC}{EB/EC}=-1$.

questions.stem: Prove that two lines are perpendicular iff the product of their slopes is $-1$ (for non-vertical lines).
solution_steps: Direction vectors are $(1,m_1)$ and $(1,m_2)$.
Lines are perpendicular iff the dot product $1\cdot1+m_1m_2=0$.
That is exactly $m_1m_2=-1$.

questions.stem: $D$ lies on $BC$. Prove $\dfrac{[ABD]}{[ACD]}=\dfrac{BD}{DC}$.
solution_steps: Both triangles $ABD,ACD$ share the apex $A$ and have bases $BD,DC$ on line $BC$.
They therefore have the same height from $A$ to $BC$.
Area $=\tfrac12\,\text{base}\times\text{height}$, so the ratio of areas equals the ratio of bases $BD:DC$.

questions.stem: Prove that the three medians divide a triangle into six smaller triangles of equal area.

hint.level_1: Use the $2:1$ centroid ratio on the small triangles.

solution_steps: A median splits the triangle into two equal areas (equal bases, same height).
The centroid divides each median in ratio $2:1$, so triangles sharing the centroid with equal bases on a median have equal areas.
Comparing adjacent pieces around $G$ shows all six are equal.
Hence each has area $\tfrac16[ABC]$.

questions.stem: Prove the shoelace formula: the area of $\triangle ABC$ with $A=(x_1,y_1)$ etc.\ is $\tfrac12|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)|$.
solution_steps: $[ABC]=\tfrac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$ (magnitude of the cross product).
The $2$D cross product is $(x_2-x_1)(y_3-y_1)-(x_3-x_1)(y_2-y_1)$.
Expanding and regrouping gives the stated symmetric expression.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$ with $CA=4,CB=5,\angle C=50^\circ$, prove $[ABC]=\tfrac12\,CA\cdot CB\sin C$ and evaluate.
solution_steps: Drop the altitude from $A$ to line $CB$; its length is $h=CA\sin C$.
Area $=\tfrac12\cdot CB\cdot h=\tfrac12\,CB\cdot CA\sin C$.
Numerically $[ABC]=\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot5\cdot\sin 50^\circ\approx 7.660$.

questions.stem: Prove the Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$, $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

hint.level_0: Use the altitude to the hypotenuse.
hint.level_1: Two similar sub-triangles; add the relations.

solution_steps: Drop the altitude $CH$ from the right angle to the hypotenuse $AB$.
$\triangle ACH\sim\triangle ABC$ gives $AC^2=AH\cdot AB$; $\triangle BCH\sim\triangle BAC$ gives $BC^2=BH\cdot AB$.
Add: $AC^2+BC^2=(AH+BH)\,AB=AB^2$.
That is $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

questions.stem: Let $P$ be a point inside an equilateral triangle. Prove the sum of the distances from $P$ to the three sides equals the altitude (Viviani's Theorem).
solution_steps: Join $P$ to the three vertices, splitting the triangle into three small triangles.
Their areas are $\tfrac12 s\,d_a,\tfrac12 s\,d_b,\tfrac12 s\,d_c$ (each side has length $s$).
Sum $=\tfrac12 s(d_a+d_b+d_c)$ equals the whole area $\tfrac12 s\,h$.
Cancel $\tfrac12 s$: $d_a+d_b+d_c=h$.

questions.stem: Equilateral triangles are erected outward on the sides of $\triangle ABC$. Prove their centers form an equilateral triangle (Napoleon's Theorem).

hint.level_1: An equilateral triangle $\iff z_1+\omega z_2+\omega^2 z_3=0$.

solution_steps: Represent the vertices as complex numbers and let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$.
The center of the outward equilateral on a side is an affine ($\omega$-weighted) combination of its endpoints.
Compute $N_a,N_b,N_c$; the condition $N_a+\omega N_b+\omega^2 N_c=0$ for an equilateral triangle holds identically.
Hence $N_aN_bN_c$ is equilateral.

questions.stem: In a triangle with all angles below $120^\circ$, erect outward equilateral triangles and join each outer apex to the opposite vertex. Prove these three lines concur at a point $F$ from which each side subtends $120^\circ$.

hint.level_0: Use a $60^\circ$ rotation about a vertex.
hint.level_1: $F$ lies on the circumcircles of the erected equilateral triangles.
hint.level_2: Each such arc gives a $120^\circ$ angle.

solution_steps: Let $A',B',C'$ be the outer apexes on $BC,CA,AB$. Rotating by $60^\circ$ about a vertex maps one of these segments to another, showing $AA'=BB'=CC'$.
The same rotation argument shows the three cevians $AA',BB',CC'$ are equal and concurrent.
At the common point $F$, the circumcircles of the equilateral triangles meet, giving $\angle BFC=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$, etc.
Hence each side subtends $120^\circ$ at $F$.
